title: The Calendar and Festivals
summary: How Israel counted days, months, and years; the Hebrew months with their Babylonian names and modern equivalents; the Sabbath, the pilgrim festivals, the Day of Atonement, Purim and Hanukkah; the calendar disputes of Jesus' day; and how the feasts shaped the Christian year.

sections.body:
Israel's day began at sunset, not at midnight. The creation account counts each day as “evening, and there was morning” (Genesis 1:5), and the Law fixes the Day of Atonement “from the evening of the ninth day of the month until the following evening” (Leviticus 23:32). Jewish practice still keeps Sabbaths and festivals from sundown to sundown. This matters for reading the Passion narratives: the Last Supper on Thursday evening and the crucifixion on Friday afternoon fell, by Jewish reckoning, on the same day, and the body of Jesus had to be taken down before sunset on Friday because the Sabbath began at dusk (Mark 15:42; John 19:31).

The daylight was divided into twelve hours from sunrise to sunset (“Are there not twelve hours of daylight?” John 11:9), so an hour was longer in summer than in winter. The third hour was about nine in the morning, the sixth about noon, and the ninth about three in the afternoon, the hour of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer in the temple (Acts 3:1). Mark marks the crucifixion by these hours: Jesus was crucified at the third hour, darkness fell from the sixth to the ninth, and he cried out at the ninth (Mark 15:25, 33-34). John's statement that Pilate's judgment came “about the sixth hour” (John 19:14) has been explained in several ways: as a rounding of the time to the nearest quarter of the day, as a difference in what the two evangelists were marking, or, less likely, as Roman reckoning from midnight. The night was divided into watches: three in the Old Testament (Judges 7:19 mentions the middle watch) and four in the Roman period, which Jesus names as evening, midnight, rooster-crow, and morning (Mark 13:35).

The seven-day week, ending in the Sabbath, is one of Israel's gifts to the world. The days had no names except the Sabbath; the others were numbered, ‘the first day of the week’ and so on, and by the first century Friday was called ‘the Preparation’ because food for the Sabbath was prepared on it. The week was not tied to the moon or the sun. It rested on a command grounded in creation, “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested” (Exodus 20:11), and in redemption, since Deuteronomy grounds the same command in the memory of slavery: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). A slave has no day off. A redeemed people, and their servants and animals, did.

Israel's months followed the moon. The Hebrew word chodesh means both ‘new moon’ and ‘month’, and each month began when the thin crescent of the new moon was first seen at sunset. A lunar month is about 29 and a half days, so months ran to 29 or 30 days, and twelve of them make about 354 days, eleven short of the solar year. Left alone, a lunar calendar drifts through the seasons, as the Islamic calendar does today. But Israel's festivals were tied to the harvest: Passover had to fall in the month of Abib, the month when the barley was in the ear, and the firstfruits of the barley had to be ready to wave before the LORD. So a thirteenth month, a second Adar, was added when needed, roughly seven times in every nineteen years. In the Second Temple period the decision was made by the priests or the court in Jerusalem, who watched the state of the barley, the fruit, and the season. According to a tradition recorded by Hai Gaon around 1000, the patriarch Hillel II published fixed rules for the calendar in AD 358 or 359, and the Jewish calendar has run by calculation rather than observation since, though the rules reached their final form only centuries later.

Israel counted two new years. The LORD told Moses at the exodus that “This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year” (Exodus 12:2), so the religious calendar, and the numbering of the months, begins in the spring with Nisan. But the farming year ran from autumn to autumn, and Exodus 23:16 places the Feast of Ingathering “at the end of the year”. The oldest Hebrew calendar inscription, the Gezer calendar from the tenth century BC, lists the farmer's months starting in the autumn: two months of ingathering, two of sowing, two of late sowing, a month of hoeing flax, a month of barley harvest, a month of harvest and measuring grain, two months of vine-tending, and a month of summer fruit. The Mishnah later counts four new years in all (Rosh Hashanah 1:1): the first of Nisan for kings and festivals, the first of Elul for the tithe of animals, the first of Tishri for the counting of years, sabbatical years, and jubilees, and the first or fifteenth of Shevat (Beth Shammai and Beth Hillel disagreed) for fruit trees. Today's Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, falls on the first of Tishri. The difference between a spring and an autumn new year is one of the reasons the dates of the kings are hard to work out, as the guide to the kings in this series explains.

The Bible uses three sets of month names. Most often it simply numbers the months: ‘the first month’, ‘the seventh month’. Four months appear with old Canaanite names, found in Exodus and in the account of Solomon's temple: Abib, Ziv, Ethanim, and Bul. After the exile, the books of Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, and Zechariah use the Babylonian names, adapted into Hebrew and Aramaic, that Jews still use: Nisan, Sivan, Elul, Kislev, Tevet, Shevat, and Adar all appear in Scripture. The rabbis themselves remembered that the month names had come up with the exiles from Babylon (Jerusalem Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 1:2). Tammuz, the name of the fourth month, was also the name of a Mesopotamian god whose death was mourned each summer, and Ezekiel was shown women “weeping for Tammuz” at the temple gate (Ezekiel 8:14).

The table sets out the twelve months in the order of the religious year, with the older Hebrew names where the Bible uses them, the Babylonian names from which the later Hebrew names come, the approximate place of each month in the modern calendar, the farming year, and the festivals. Because the months are lunar, each one overlaps two modern months and shifts by a few weeks from year to year. The agricultural notes describe the land of Israel, where rain falls from about October to April and the summer is dry: the ‘early rain’ of autumn softened the ground for plowing and the ‘latter rain’ of spring filled out the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14).

Two months of the table, Tammuz and Av, are never named in the Bible, which speaks only of the fourth and fifth months. Their names are known from later Jewish sources and from the Babylonian calendar. Several festivals marked in brackets are later than the Old Testament: the fasts that grew out of the fall of Jerusalem, Hanukkah, and the rabbinic new year for trees.

sections.h: Sabbath, new moon, sabbatical year, and Jubilee
sections.body:
The Sabbath was the heartbeat of Israel's time. It is the only festival in the Ten Commandments, and Exodus calls it a sign between God and Israel “so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (Exodus 31:13). Its core was rest from ordinary work, for the whole household, including servants, foreigners, and animals. By the first century, Jewish teachers had worked out in detail what counted as work, since Scripture forbids it without defining it; the Mishnah lists thirty-nine main categories of forbidden labor (Shabbat 7:2). Most of Jesus' conflicts with Pharisees over the Sabbath concern not whether to keep it but how: healing, plucking grain, carrying a mat. His principle, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27), was not unlike some rabbinic sayings, but he joined it to the claim that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

The new moon was a lesser holy day, marked by trumpets and extra sacrifices (Numbers 10:10; 28:11-15). Saul held a feast at the new moon (1 Samuel 20:5), and Amos's merchants resented it, along with the Sabbath, because it stopped trade (Amos 8:5).

The Sabbath principle extended to years. Every seventh year the land was to lie fallow, its natural growth left for the poor and the animals (Exodus 23:10-11; Leviticus 25:1-7), and Deuteronomy adds a release of debts in that year (Deuteronomy 15:1-11). The Chronicler reads the seventy years of exile as the land finally receiving the Sabbaths it had been denied (2 Chronicles 36:21), and Nehemiah's community pledged to keep the seventh year (Nehemiah 10:31). By the second century BC, the sabbatical year was observed: 1 Maccabees 6:49, 53 mentions food shortages because it was a sabbatical year, and Josephus refers to it as well. After seven sabbatical cycles came the Jubilee, the fiftieth year, announced by the ram's horn on the Day of Atonement, when land returned to its ancestral families and Israelite debt-slaves went free (Leviticus 25:8-55). Whether the Jubilee was ever observed as the Law describes is uncertain; the Old Testament never records one, and scholars differ on whether it was an ideal, an older practice later lost, or a law regularly evaded. Its language of liberty lies behind Isaiah 61:1-2, which Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth to announce his own mission: “to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor” (Luke 4:19).

Three times a year every Israelite man was to “appear before the LORD your God in the place He will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles” (Deuteronomy 16:16). These were the pilgrim festivals, and each joined a moment in the farming year to a moment in Israel's story. In the first century they filled Jerusalem with pilgrims from Galilee and from the Jewish communities scattered across the Roman and Parthian worlds, which is why Acts 2 can list visitors from some fifteen lands and peoples at Pentecost.

Passover and Unleavened Bread began the year. On the fourteenth of Nisan, toward evening, the Passover lambs were slaughtered, and that night families ate the meal of lamb, unleavened bread, and bitter herbs, remembering the night of the exodus when the LORD passed over the houses marked with blood (Exodus 12). The seven days of Unleavened Bread followed, from the fifteenth to the twenty-first, with all leaven removed from the house. In Deuteronomy the Passover is to be sacrificed only at the central sanctuary (Deuteronomy 16:5-6), and the great Passovers of Hezekiah and Josiah were remembered as national renewals (2 Chronicles 30; 2 Kings 23:21-23). In Jesus' day the lambs were slaughtered in the temple courts and eaten in homes and rented rooms across the city. The Mishnah's tractate Pesachim describes the meal, including cups of wine and the singing of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113 to 118), though how much of that order goes back before AD 70 is debated.

During the festival, the first sheaf of the barley harvest was waved before the LORD “on the day after the Sabbath” (Leviticus 23:11), and no new grain could be eaten until then. Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), since Jesus rose on the Sunday of Passover week. From that day seven weeks were counted to the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), the fiftieth day, which Greek-speaking Jews called Pentecost (‘fiftieth’). It celebrated the wheat harvest with two loaves of leavened bread (Leviticus 23:15-21). Later Jewish tradition connected it with the giving of the Law at Sinai, which Exodus 19:1 places in the third month; the book of Jubilees, from the second century BC, already links the festival to covenant-making. At this festival the Spirit was poured out on the disciples (Acts 2:1-4).

Tabernacles, or Booths (Sukkot), was the great autumn feast of ingathering, from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of Tishri, with a closing assembly on the eighth day. Israel lived for a week in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness years (Leviticus 23:39-43), and it was the most joyful of the festivals; Solomon dedicated the temple at it (1 Kings 8:2), and the returned exiles rediscovered it under Ezra (Nehemiah 8:13-18). Zechariah foresaw the nations coming up to Jerusalem to keep it (Zechariah 14:16). By the first century it included a daily procession carrying water from the Pool of Siloam to pour at the altar, and great lamps lit in the Court of the Women (Mishnah, Sukkah 4:9 to 5:4). Against that background Jesus stood up “on the last and greatest day of the feast” and invited the thirsty to come to him and drink (John 7:37), and soon after declared himself the light of the world (John 8:12).

sections.h: Trumpets and the Day of Atonement
sections.body:
The seventh month opened with a holy day announced by trumpet blasts (Leviticus 23:23-25; Numbers 29:1-6). The Bible gives it no further explanation, and the name ‘Rosh Hashanah’, the head of the year, is later; in the Mishnah it has become the new year for counting years, a day of judgment on which the ram's horn (shofar) is blown. It opens the ten solemn days that lead to the Day of Atonement.

The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), on the tenth of the seventh month, was the most solemn day of the year. It was a day of complete rest and fasting (Israel was to “humble yourselves”, Leviticus 23:27), and the only day on which the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, carrying incense and the blood of a bull for himself and of a goat for the people. A second goat, the goat ‘for Azazel’ (traditionally ‘the scapegoat’), had the people's sins confessed over it and was sent into the wilderness (Leviticus 16). The day cleansed the sanctuary itself of the uncleanness and sin of a year, “because on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD.” (Leviticus 16:30). By the first century it was known simply as ‘the Fast’, which is how Luke dates the dangerous season of Paul's voyage (Acts 27:9), since it fell in September or October, near the end of safe sailing. The Letter to the Hebrews reads Christ's death and ascension through this day, as the high priest's once-for-all entry into the true sanctuary with his own blood (Hebrews 9:6-14, 24-28). The guide to offerings and purity in this series treats the ritual more fully.

Two festivals were added after the Law of Moses, both remembering a deliverance. Purim, on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, celebrates the rescue of the Jews of the Persian Empire told in the book of Esther. Its name comes from pur, a Babylonian word for the lot that Haman cast to choose the day of their destruction: “Therefore these days are called Purim, from the word Pur.” (Esther 9:26). Mordecai and Esther established it as days “of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor” (Esther 9:22). It is still kept by reading the scroll of Esther aloud in the synagogue, with the congregation drowning out Haman's name.

Hanukkah, the Feast of Dedication, celebrates the recovery and rededication of the temple by Judas Maccabeus on the twenty-fifth of Kislev in 164 BC, three years after the Seleucid king Antiochus IV had set up a pagan altar on the altar of burnt offering (1 Maccabees 4:52-59; 2 Maccabees 10:5-8). The celebration lasted eight days, which 2 Maccabees compares to Tabernacles, and Josephus calls it the festival of Lights. The later story of a single day's oil burning for eight days appears in the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 21b), centuries afterward. John records that Jesus was in the temple, in Solomon's Colonnade, at “the Feast of Dedication” in winter (John 10:22), where he was asked to say plainly whether he was the Christ and answered, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). At the festival of the rededicated temple, he spoke of himself as “the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world” (John 10:36).

Israel also remembered disasters. After the fall of Jerusalem the exiles fasted in the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months, and Zechariah was asked whether the fasts should continue now that the temple was rebuilt; the LORD's answer promised that they “will become times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts for the house of Judah” (Zechariah 8:19). In Jewish tradition these became the fast of the seventeenth of Tammuz (the breach of the walls), the ninth of Av (Tisha b'Av, the destruction of both the first and the second temples), the fast of Gedaliah in Tishri (the murder of the governor, Jeremiah 41), and the tenth of Tevet (the beginning of the siege, 2 Kings 25:1).

sections.body:
Jews in the Second Temple period did not all keep the same calendar, and the disagreements were bitter because they meant keeping God's appointed days on the wrong days. The book of Jubilees and the astronomical part of 1 Enoch, both from the third or second century BC, defend a solar calendar of 364 days, exactly fifty-two weeks, in which every festival falls on the same day of the week every year. The community whose library was found at Qumran by the Dead Sea kept this calendar and accused the Jerusalem priesthood of following the moon and profaning the festivals. A document from Qumran records the high priest (‘the Wicked Priest’) coming to confront the community's leader on what was, by the community's calendar, their Day of Atonement (1QpHab 11.4-8).

Even those who used the lunar calendar disagreed about details. The count to Pentecost begins “on the day after the Sabbath” (Leviticus 23:11, 15), and the Pharisees read ‘Sabbath’ there as the first day of Unleavened Bread, a festival rest day, so that the sheaf was waved on the sixteenth of Nisan whatever the day of the week. The Sadducees (or, in rabbinic sources, the Boethusians) read it as the weekly Sabbath, so that the sheaf and Pentecost always fell on a Sunday. The Babylonian Talmud records the rabbis' arguments against them (Menachot 65a-66a).

The best-known calendar question in the New Testament concerns the date of the Last Supper. Matthew, Mark, and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal, eaten on the evening that began the fifteenth of Nisan (Mark 14:12-16). John places the crucifixion on “the day of Preparation for the Passover” (John 19:14), with the Jewish leaders not yet having eaten the Passover when they brought Jesus to Pilate (John 18:28), so that Jesus died as the Passover lambs were being slaughtered on the afternoon of the fourteenth. Joachim Jeremias (The Eucharistic Words of Jesus) argued at length that the Last Supper was a Passover meal. John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 1, 1991) and others hold that John's chronology is historically right and that the Synoptic writers presented the meal in Passover terms for theological reasons. Annie Jaubert (La date de la Cène, 1957) proposed that Jesus kept Passover by the 364-day calendar of Jubilees, earlier in the week, and Colin Humphreys (The Mystery of the Last Supper, 2011) has proposed a different older calendar. Others, including many conservative commentators, argue that John's phrases can refer to the whole Passover week rather than the day of the lamb, so that the Gospels agree. All sides agree that Jesus died at Passover, on a Friday, and that the Gospels, each in its own way, present his death as the true Passover: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

sections.h: The festivals and the Christian year
sections.body:
The New Testament reads Israel's calendar as fulfilled in Christ without simply cancelling it. Jesus kept the festivals and went up to Jerusalem for them; his death fell at Passover, his resurrection on the Sunday of Passover week, which Paul links with the firstfruits, and the Spirit came at Pentecost. Paul still planned his travel around Pentecost (Acts 20:16; 1 Corinthians 16:8). At the same time Paul warned gentile believers not to let anyone judge them “with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.” (Colossians 2:16-17), and he left observance of days to the conscience of each believer (Romans 14:5). Hebrews speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for God's people, entered by faith (Hebrews 4:9-11).

The early church met on ‘the first day of the week’ (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), the day of the resurrection, which Revelation 1:10 calls ‘the Lord's day’. Christians have since understood the relation of Sunday to the Sabbath in several ways. The Reformed and Puritan tradition, set out in the Westminster Confession (1646), holds that the fourth commandment is moral and permanent and that the Christian Sabbath moved to the first day of the week at the resurrection. Many Lutherans, Anglicans, Catholics, and others see the Sabbath command as fulfilled in Christ, with Sunday worship kept as a joyful gathering and a rule of the church rather than as the Sabbath transferred. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that the seventh day remains binding. Each view appeals to Scripture, and each is held by faithful Christians.

Easter grew directly out of Passover, and in many languages its name still comes from the Hebrew pesach (Pâques, Pascua, Pasqua). In the second century some churches of Asia Minor, the ‘Quartodecimans’ (‘fourteenth-ers’), kept Easter on the fourteenth of Nisan whatever the weekday, while Rome and most others kept it on the following Sunday; Eusebius records the dispute between Polycrates of Ephesus and Victor of Rome around 190 (Church History 5.23-25). The Council of Nicaea in 325 agreed that the whole church should keep Easter on a Sunday and compute it independently of the Jewish calendar. Pentecost, too, passed into the Christian year as the feast of the Spirit, fifty days after Easter. The Christian calendar that shapes much of the world still runs, underneath, on the rhythm of Israel's feasts.
